In the random greedy process, we iteratively select $ r $-cliques uniformly at random, ensuring that the resulting hypergraph remains linear and has girth greater than $ \ell $. The process continues until no more such cliques can be added. The number of edges $ M $ in the final hypergraph is then the quantity of interest.

The family $\{\Sigma_{(v,t)}\}_{(v,t) \in \mathring{B}^4 \times [-\pi, \pi]}$ is defined as the boundary of the set $\{x \mid d_v(x) < t\}$, forming a five-parameter family of surfaces associated with $\Sigma$.

The key result is that the maximum area among all $\Sigma_{(v,t)}$ is bounded above by $2\pi^2$, and this bound is achieved if and only if $\Sigma$ is the Clifford torus. The Clifford torus is a well-known minimal surface in $\mathbb{S}^3$ with area $2\pi^2$, and it is the only surface for which this maximum is attained.

The strongest known results in this area, particularly in the context of von Neumann algebras and group theory, suggest that it is possible to construct a family of $ W^* $-McDuff groups of size $ 2^{\aleph_0} $, each of which is McDuff superrigid in the strongest sense. Thus, the strongest existence statement that can be proved is that there exists a family of $ W^* $-McDuff groups of size $ 2^{\aleph_0} $, with pairwise non-isomorphic groups, each of which is McDuff superrigid in the strongest sense.

This is a stronger condition than simply being an initial colex-segment or being relabel-isomorphic to an initial lex-segment.
